title: Sampling backwards
objectives: Write the reverse sampling loop, and check its samples against the data.

screens.title: Rings out of noise
screens.prose: Start from 300 points drawn from a standard normal, a round cloud. At each step the trained noise predictor of l14 removes its guess of the noise, and a little fresh noise is added. Slide from step 50 down to step 0.
screens.question: When do the two rings become clear?

options.text: Only in the last few steps, after step 10
Within the first ten steps, by step 40
options.why: At step 30 the cloud is still round. The rings sharpen at the very end.

options.text: Halfway, at step 25
options.why: At step 20 there is a blurred cloud, not two rings.

options.text: Never: the samples stay a round cloud
options.why: Slide to step 0: two rings appear.

hints.text: Compare steps 10, 5 and 0.
Most of the structure arrives at the end.

feedback.correct: Right. The share of points near a ring stays near 0.24 until step 10, then reaches 0.70 at step 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide through the last few steps.

explain.text: Early reverse steps mostly shrink the cloud and set its broad shape; the fine structure, the gap between the rings, appears in the last steps, where the noise is small. At step 0, 0.70 of the points lie within 0.1 of a ring.

screens.title: One step back
screens.prose: The **reverse step** is $$\mathbf{x}_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(\mathbf{x}_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\Big) + \sigma_t\mathbf{z},\quad \sigma_t^2 = \beta_t.$$ At $t = 10$: $\beta_{10} \approx 0.03755$, $\bar\alpha_{10} \approx 0.82255$. Take $\mathbf{x}_{10} = (0.9, 0.2)$, net output $(0.3, -0.5)$ and $\mathbf{z} = (0.1, 0.4)$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{x}_9$, to 3 decimal places.

hints.text: $\beta_{10}/\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{10}} \approx 0.0891$ and $1/\sqrt{\alpha_{10}} \approx 1.0193$.
$\sigma_{10} = \sqrt{\beta_{10}} \approx 0.1938$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove the scaled noise guess, divide by $\sqrt{\alpha_{10}}$, then add $\sigma_{10}\mathbf{z}$.

byKey.nonoise: That is the mean alone; add $\sigma_{10}\mathbf{z}$.

explain.text: The mean is $(0.890, 0.249)$; adding $\sqrt{\beta_{10}}\,\mathbf{z}$ gives $(0.910, 0.327)$. Fifty such steps turn noise into a sample.

screens.title: Check the samples
screens.prose: A sample statistic: the **ring share**, the fraction of points within 0.1 of either ring's radius. The bars compare 1,000 samples with the data and with a round normal cloud of the data's variance, 0.8 per coordinate.
screens.question: What fraction of the samples land near a ring? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: Read the samples' bar.
Compare it with the round normal's.

feedback.correct: About 0.70, against 0.21 for a round cloud and 1 for the data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the samples' bar.

byKey.base: That is the round normal cloud, the share with no structure at all.
byKey.data: That is the data's own share.

explain.text: The samples land near a ring 0.70 of the time, far above the 0.21 of a structureless cloud but short of the data. A statistic like this, checked on held-out data, is how a sampler is judged.

screens.title: Leave out the fresh noise
screens.prose: A colleague drops $\sigma_t\mathbf{z}$ from every step, reasoning that noise can only blur the samples. The chart shows their 300 samples; only the first draw is random.
screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The samples collapse onto the inner ring: 0% reach the outer one
Nothing: the samples are simply sharper versions of the right ones
options.why: They are sharper but wrong: the outer ring, half of the data, vanishes (0%).

options.text: The samples come out blurred into one cloud
options.why: Without the noise they pile up, not spread out.

options.text: Sampling becomes slower without the noise
options.why: The cost is the same; the distribution of samples is what changes.

hints.text: Count the points on the outer ring.
With the noise, 50% are out there.

feedback.correct: Right. The added noise is what lets samples spread over the whole distribution.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the two rings in the chart.

byKey.sharper: You read sharp as good. A sampler must also cover every part of the data.

explain.text: Each step's mean pulls points towards likely places; without fresh noise every path follows the strongest pull and the outer ring empties to 0%. The $\sigma_t\mathbf{z}$ term keeps the spread that the forward process had.

screens.title: The direction matters
screens.prose: Someone runs the same reverse steps but with $t$ counting up from 1 to 50. Their ring share is 0.22.
screens.question: Why does it fail?

options.text: Each step applies the net at the wrong noise level
It should not fail: the steps are the same either way
options.why: The steps differ by their $t$: each step's size and the net's guess depend on it. The share, 0.22, is no better than a round cloud.

options.text: Too much fresh noise is added at the end
options.why: The noise schedule is the issue only because it is applied in the wrong order.

options.text: The net was trained on the wrong data
options.why: The same net works when $t$ runs down.

hints.text: What does the net assume about $\mathbf{x}_t$ at $t = 1$?
At $t = 1$, $\mathbf{x}_t$ is nearly the data.

feedback.correct: Right. The reverse chain must run from $T$ down to 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what the net expects at each $t$.

explain.text: Each step undoes the forward step with the same $t$. Run upwards, the first steps remove tiny noise from a pure-noise cloud, and the share stays at 0.22.

screens.title: A start far out in the tail
screens.prose: Two runs use the same fresh noise at every step but different starts: $(3.5, 3.5)$, far out in the normal's tail, and the origin. They end at radii 1.68 and 1.67.
screens.question: What does this say about the starting point?

options.text: Fresh noise and the net matter more than the start
Tail starts always land outside the outer ring
options.why: This one ends at radius 1.68, on the outer ring, beside the run from the origin.

options.text: Tail starts land between the rings
options.why: Some may, by chance; this one landed on the outer ring like the run from the origin.

options.text: The final point copies the starting point
options.why: The two runs started 4.9 apart and ended close together.

hints.text: Compare the two final radii.
The two runs shared their noise draws.

feedback.correct: Right. Early steps shrink away the start; the last steps decide where a point lands.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare where the two runs ended.

explain.text: The reverse chain shrinks the start by roughly $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_T} \approx 0.067$ in effect, so a tail start is soon forgotten. Its point can still land in an odd place by chance, which is why samples are judged as a group.

screens.title: The sampling loop
screens.prose: Draw $\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. For $t = T, \ldots, 1$: $$\mathbf{x}_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(\mathbf{x}_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\Big) + \sigma_t\mathbf{z}_t,$$ with fresh $\mathbf{z}_t$, $\sigma_t^2 = \beta_t$ (one of Ho et al.'s two choices), and no noise at the last step.
screens.question: Why is no noise added at $t = 1$?

options.text: It is the sample itself; noise would only blur it
Because $\beta_1 = 0$
options.why: $\beta_1 = 0.001$ here, small but not 0; the choice is a convention for the final output.

options.text: Adding it would make the loop diverge
options.why: One small extra draw cannot make the loop diverge; it would just blur the output.

explain.text: Noise at earlier steps keeps samples spread over the distribution; at the final step it would only add blur of size $\sqrt{\beta_1}$.

screens.prose: Write the reverse step with the module's `eps_model`. Index the schedule with `t - 1`, and skip the fresh noise when `t == 1`.
screens.question: Write `reverse_step`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import representations_ops_l4 as ops


def reverse_step(x, t, params, betas, abar, z):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    betas = np.asarray(betas, dtype=float)
    abar = np.asarray(abar, dtype=float)
    T = len(betas)
    beta, a_bar = betas[t - 1], abar[t - 1]
    eps = ops.eps_model(params, x, t, T)
    mean = (x - beta / np.sqrt(1.0 - a_bar) * eps) / np.sqrt(1.0 - beta)
    if t > 1:
        return mean + np.sqrt(beta) * np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    return mean

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import representations_ops_l4 as ops


def sample(params, betas, n, seed):
    betas = np.asarray(betas, dtype=float)
    T = len(betas)
    abar = np.cumprod(1.0 - betas)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = rng.standard_normal((n, 2))
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        eps = ops.eps_model(params, x, t, T)
        x = (x - betas[t - 1] / np.sqrt(1.0 - abar[t - 1]) * eps) / np.sqrt(1.0 - betas[t - 1])
        if t > 1:
            x = x + np.sqrt(betas[t - 1]) * rng.standard_normal((n, 2))
    return x

screens.title: Scenarios that look like history
screens.prose: A risk team trains a diffusion model on ten years of daily returns of 20 assets and samples 50,000 synthetic days for a stress test. A colleague checks that the samples reproduce the training data's volatilities and correlations.
screens.question: What is the more important check?

options.text: Compare the samples' statistics with held-out days the model never saw
The training-data check is enough, since the model learned from it
options.why: A model can reproduce its training data closely and still fail on new days, or simply copy training days.

options.text: Plot a few samples and check they look realistic
options.why: A few realistic-looking days say little about tails, correlations under stress, or copying.

options.text: Draw more samples until the statistics settle
options.why: More samples tighten the estimates of the model's statistics, not their match to reality.

hints.text: What could go wrong that training data cannot reveal?
Copying and overfitting look perfect on training data.

feedback.correct: Right. Judge a generator on data it did not train on.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the training-data check cannot reveal.

explain.text: Matching the training data is necessary, not sufficient: a model that memorised days would pass it. Held-out statistics, and a check for near-copies of training days, test whether the model generalises.

ideas: The reverse step removes the scaled noise guess, divides by $\sqrt{\alpha_t}$ and adds fresh noise of variance $\beta_t$, except at the last step; the loop runs from $T$ down to 1.
Samples are judged by a statistic against the data: here 0.70 of samples land near a ring, against 0.21 for a structureless cloud.
Without the fresh noise the samples collapse onto the strongest part of the data; run upwards, the chain uses the wrong noise levels.
